clue.text: What may be raised with pride?

definitions.text: What may be raised with pride?

parts.words: What may be raised with pride?
parts.note: surface reading: something a person brings up with a feeling of satisfaction, like a child or a flag
setter's reading: a pride is a group of lions, and its young are reared within it

explanation.surface: A proud parent wonders what is worth bringing up with satisfaction.
explanation.walkthrough: Pride here is the collective noun for lions, not the feeling; the young animals are raised in that group.
explanation.definitionFit: Young lions are reared within the family group called a pride, so they are literally brought up in one.

clue.text: The French deserter comprehending one with rope

parts.note: la is French for the, feminine form

indicators.note: comprehending in its old sense means including or taking in, so one piece holds another

parts.note: a rat is someone who deserts their side
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A French deserter, understanding someone, makes off with a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: A lariat is a lasso, a long noosed rope used for catching livestock.

clue.text: Reference book has one page on American person who married his mother

parts.note: the Oxford English Dictionary, the classic reference book
the Roman numeral for one
P is the abbreviation for page
US for American

explanation.surface: A dictionary entry has a page about an American who wed his own mother.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Oedipus unknowingly killed his father and married his mother Jocasta, as told by Sophocles.

clue.text: Study position of European lake

parts.note: to con is an old word meaning to study or learn
a stance is a position or posture

explanation.surface: Someone researches where a lake on the Continent lies.
explanation.definitionFit: Lake Constance, the Bodensee, lies on the Rhine where Germany, Austria and Switzerland meet.

clue.text: A regular flasher in the High Street?

definitions.text: A regular flasher in the High Street?

parts.words: A regular flasher in the High Street?
parts.note: surface reading: a man who habitually exposes himself in a town's main shopping street
setter's reading: a lamp that blinks on and off at steady intervals beside a road crossing

explanation.surface: A habitual exhibitionist haunts a town's main shopping street.
explanation.walkthrough: A flasher is slang for an exhibitionist, but here it is a light that flashes; High Street is the British name for a town's main street.
explanation.definitionFit: Belisha beacons are the flashing amber globes on poles marking zebra pedestrian crossings in Britain, found on busy streets.

clue.text: Celebrity attending church ceremony

parts.note: a celebrity is a star
CH is the standard abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A famous person turns up at a church service.
explanation.definitionFit: Starch in the figurative sense is stiff formality of manner, a synonym for ceremony as in standing on ceremony.

clue.text: Finish of match at university

parts.note: a tie is a match, as in a cup tie
a student in residence is said to be up at university

explanation.surface: A sporting fixture ends at a university ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finish of match' reads as the end of a game, but 'finish' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie-up is a conclusion or bringing together of loose ends, so a finishing, as in to tie up a deal.

clue.text: Old soldier cared to abroad

indicators.note: abroad can mean astray or widely scattered, so the letters wander into a new order

parts.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A veteran soldier had wanted to serve overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: Redcoat was the name for a British soldier of past centuries, from the scarlet uniform.

clue.text: At this place for opening of dealership in English city

parts.note: here means at this place
taken as written

indicators.note: an opening is a beginning, so only the initial letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the initial letter of dealership

explanation.surface: A car dealership is opening a branch here, in an English city.
explanation.definitionFit: Hereford is a cathedral city in the West Midlands of England, near the Welsh border.

clue.text: Right old racket made by sculptor

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
O is the abbreviation for old
a racket is a loud noise, a din

explanation.surface: A sculptor's studio produces a real old-fashioned commotion.
explanation.definitionFit: Auguste Rodin, maker of The Thinker, is a famous French sculptor, so he is an example of the type.

clue.text: I see what you're saying

parts.note: surface reading: the everyday phrase meaning I understand you
setter's reading: a person who literally watches speech, following the mouth's movements, rather than hearing it

explanation.surface: Someone in conversation signals that they follow the other person's point.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means 'I understand'; read literally, the speaker is watching the words being formed.
explanation.definitionFit: A deaf or hard-of-hearing person who interprets speech by watching mouth movements does literally see what is said.

clue.text: Equipment in a plane, almost hairy, terribly below standard

parts.note: par is the standard or normal level, as in golf

indicators.note: terribly suggests something done badly or chaotically, so the letters are jumbled
almost means not quite all, so the final letter of the word after it is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, before trimming

explanation.surface: A plane's equipment is in such terrible condition that it is not up to scratch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Below standard' looks like a judgement on quality, but in a down clue it places the jumbled letters beneath a word for standard.
explanation.definitionFit: Paraphernalia means the miscellaneous gear and articles needed for an activity, which is equipment.

clue.text: Praise cooking, eating favourite dim sum?

indicators.note: something that eats takes another thing inside itself, so one piece goes into the other
cooking works ingredients into something new, so the letters of the first word get mixed up

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
a favourite is a pet, as in teacher's pet

explanation.surface: A diner praises the cooking of their favourite dim sum.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags dim sum as an example: these small dishes are often eaten as a starter.
explanation.definitionFit: Dim sum are small dumplings and bites often served before a meal, so they are an example of a starter course.

clue.text: Demonstration in prison, initially on top of building

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word just before it

parts.note: the opening letter of prison
the roof is the top of a building

explanation.surface: A protest staged inside a jail begins with inmates up on the roof.
explanation.walkthrough: A rooftop prison protest is the picture, but 'on' is just glue putting the first letter before the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A proof is a demonstration that something is true, as in a mathematical proof.

clue.text: Artist shown in the Observer, say, with rope

parts.note: the Observer is a British newspaper published on Sundays, so it is an example of a Sunday
a painter is the rope at a boat's bow used for tying it up

explanation.surface: An artist's work appears in the Observer newspaper, together with a rope.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'Sunday' is a Sunday newspaper, and the Observer is one; 'painter' is also a nautical word for a mooring rope.
explanation.definitionFit: A Sunday painter is an amateur who paints in spare time, so an artist, though not a professional one.

clue.text: See popular French author with two small sons in Scotland

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
Jules Verne, the French writer of Around the World in Eighty Days
S is the abbreviation for son, given twice

explanation.surface: Look at a well-loved French writer travelling with his two little boys in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like an instruction to look, but it is a bishop's seat; 'in Scotland' completes the definition by placing it.
explanation.definitionFit: A see is a bishop's seat or diocese, and Inverness has a cathedral that is a seat of a Scottish bishop.

clue.text: Child has a short sleep, reportedly, after drop of some strong drink

indicators.note: a drop is a tiny amount, so only one letter, the first, is taken from the next word

parts.note: the first letter of some
CH is the abbreviation for child

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is spoken or heard, so a word is spelt to match its sound

parts.note: someone who naps has a short sleep, and the spelling here only matches it in sound

explanation.surface: A child takes a nap after a drop of strong liquor.
explanation.definitionFit: Schnapps is a strong distilled spirit, often fruit-flavoured, from Germany and Scandinavia.

clue.text: A person from Beijing doesn't eat pak choi?

parts.note: someone from Beijing is Chinese
a diner who does not eat food leaves it on the plate

explanation.surface: A visitor from Beijing refuses to eat a plate of pak choi.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks pak choi as an example of the vegetables, which are related cabbages.
explanation.definitionFit: Chinese leaves is the name for Chinese cabbages, and pak choi is one such leafy brassica, so it is an example.

clue.text: Temporary home — Hilary, perhaps, is to be shown round one

parts.note: in means at home

indicators.note: something shown round surrounds another, so the second piece encloses the numeral

parts.note: Hilary is the spring term at Oxford and some other British universities and courts
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A woman called Hilary is shown round a temporary house.
explanation.walkthrough: Hilary looks like a person's name; it is the name of an academic term at Oxford, running from January to March.
explanation.definitionFit: Interim means provisional or for the time being, a synonym for temporary.

clue.text: Cross sailor, Irish one on being turfed out

indicators.note: turfed out means thrown out, so the named letters are removed from the word

parts.note: an old salt is a sailor
IR is the abbreviation for Irish
taken as written, before removal
the letters to be thrown out

explanation.surface: An angry sailor, an Irishman, is thrown out of somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like an adjective for the angry sailor, but it is the definition, a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A saltire is a diagonal X-shaped cross in heraldry, as on the Scottish flag of St Andrew.

clue.text: Secret hide close to nest

parts.note: to cover is to hide

indicators.note: close here means the end, so only the final letter of the next word is taken

parts.note: the final letter of nest

explanation.surface: A bird's secret hiding place is near its nest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' looks like 'near', but means the end of the word; a hide is also a birdwatchers' shelter.
explanation.definitionFit: Covert means hidden or not openly acknowledged, a synonym for secret.

clue.text: Some women at a laundry in a former SA province

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words, so the letters sit inside them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of women, all of at and a, and the start of laundry

explanation.surface: A few women work at a laundry in a South African region.
explanation.definitionFit: Natal was a province of South Africa until 1994, when it was merged into KwaZulu-Natal.

clue.text: Free, last of concerts in Cornish town

indicators.note: in places one item inside another, so the letter goes within the town's name

parts.note: Looe is a fishing town on the south coast of Cornwall

indicators.note: last of points to the final letter of the following word

parts.note: the final letter of concerts

explanation.surface: The final concert in a Cornish town is free to attend.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose means not tied up or confined, a synonym of free as in the dog got free.

clue.text: Singer, trained at control

indicators.note: something trained has been worked into a new shape, so the letters that follow are reshaped

parts.note: the letters taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A vocalist who has had training exercises good command of the voice.
explanation.definitionFit: A contralto is the lowest female voice, and so a type of singer.

clue.text: Staff venting spleen on head of research

indicators.note: venting suggests letting things out in a burst, so the words are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: 'head of' keeps only the first letter of 'research'

parts.note: the opening letter of research

explanation.surface: Employees angrily vent their frustration on the boss of the research department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Venting spleen' reads as one idiom for venting anger, but the spleen is fodder and venting the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Personnel are the people employed by an organisation, its staff.

clue.text: One banished from former French island

parts.note: ex means former
île is French for island

explanation.surface: Someone was expelled from an island that used to be French.
explanation.definitionFit: An exile is a person forced to live away from their homeland, someone banished.

clue.text: Book US male in variety

indicators.note: in variety means in a varied form, so the letters appear in a different order

parts.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A book about an American man appearing in a variety show.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel is one of the books of the Old Testament, named for the prophet.

clue.text: Criticise male in group with record of arrests

parts.note: to rap is to criticise sharply

indicators.note: in places one item inside another, so the word for a man sits within the word for a group

parts.note: a set is a group
he is the male pronoun

explanation.surface: Someone attacks a man in a gang who has a criminal record.
explanation.definitionFit: A rap sheet is American slang for a person's police record listing past arrests.
